Wikipedia article recommender¶

Information Retrieval project, Poznan University of Technology
Authors: Mateusz Niezgódka (164224), Jakub Banasiak (164184)

What the tool does¶

You give it a list of Wikipedia articles you have read. It answers with other articles you will probably find interesting.

  • Input: article titles or URLs, in any mix, e.g. ["Jazz", "Blues", "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll"].
  • Output: a ranked list of articles from a collection of 2,200 Wikipedia pages. Each has a link, a score from 0 to 1 (higher means more similar to what you read) and charts that explain the score.

How it works, in short¶

  1. Collect 2,200 Wikipedia articles on 11 broad topics and save their text (section 1).
  2. Prepare the text: clean it, split it into words and reduce each word to its dictionary form, e.g. cities → city (section 2).
  3. Score every article by how similar it is to the ones you read, using two measures: shared words and similar meaning (section 3).
  4. Recommend the best-scoring articles and explain each score (section 4).

Sections 5 and 6 describe the collection and measure how well the recommender works.

How to try it¶

  • Notebook: open notebooks/02_recommender_demo.ipynb, put your articles in VISITED and run all cells.
  • Command line: uv run python -m wiki_recommender.recommender "Dog" "Cat" -k 10

Installation is described in README.md. Every chart in this report is computed when the notebook runs, and a copy of each is saved in reports/figures/.

1. Collecting the articles¶

Source. Wikipedia's Vital articles lists (levels 4 and 5) sort about 50,000 important articles into 11 topics and many smaller subsections. We use these lists rather than following random links because they give a broad set of substantial articles, and each article comes labelled with its topic and subsection. Section 6 uses these labels to check whether recommendations are related.

Selection. Each topic gets 200 articles:

  1. the most important ones (levels 1–3, such as World War II or Dog) are always included;
  2. the rest is 60 % level 4 and 40 % level 5 articles (narrower subjects);
  3. subsections take turns, so no single subsection fills the quota.

Skipped pages. Disambiguation pages, duplicates (redirects), lists (List of ..., Outline of ...) and pages shorter than 100 words.

Scraping. Each page is downloaded through the Wikipedia API and reduced to plain text: tables, infoboxes, formulas, citation marks and closing sections such as See also or References are removed. The title, URL, introduction, section headings, categories and links are stored separately in data/raw/articles_raw.parquet.

  value
articles 2,200
candidates in the lists 49,747
topics 11
subsections 1,329
categories 15,638
words in total 13,074,491
median words per article 5,196

Every topic has exactly 200 articles. The share of level 5 articles differs between topics because the Vital articles lists differ in size.

2. Preparing the text: lemmatization and stemming¶

The raw text is turned into a list of meaningful words, so that articles can be compared word by word.

  1. Clean. Remove leftovers of the page markup (URLs, HTML tags, wiki brackets). Drop categories that describe Wikipedia itself, such as Living people.
  2. Split into words with spaCy (en_core_web_sm).
  3. Filter. Lower-case and remove accents (Müller = muller). Remove stopwords (the, and, ...), punctuation, numbers and years. Keep acronyms such as US or WHO, and words such as covid-19.
  4. Normalise every word in two ways:
    • lemma: its dictionary form, chosen by spaCy from the word's role in the sentence (studies → study);
    • stem: the word with its ending cut off by the Snowball stemmer (studies → studi).
  5. Fix guessed lemmas. For unknown words spaCy guesses the lemma by cutting a plural ending, which gives errors such as cryptocurrencies → cryptocurrencie or series → serie. After all articles are read, a guess is kept only if the singular form really appears in the collection (at least a tenth as often as the plural). 4,413 lemmas were fixed this way.

The result is saved in data/processed/articles_processed.parquet: for each article its lemmas, its stems, its definition (the first full paragraph, which says what the subject is) and its categories.

Lemmas or stems? We use lemmas. Stemming shrinks the vocabulary more (first chart), but it also merges unrelated words: universe and university both become univers, and united and unit both become unit, which is why unit appears among the most frequent stems. Lemmas are real words, so the charts and explanations stay readable. They also find related articles slightly better (section 6.1).

3. How articles are scored¶

3.1 Similarity of two articles¶

Two articles are compared in two ways. Each gives a number from 0 (nothing in common) to 1 (identical):

Measure What it captures How it works Weight
Text (TF-IDF) shared words Each article becomes a list of word weights. A word weighs more when it is frequent in the article but rare in the collection. 0.55
Embedding similar meaning A small language model (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5) turns the title and the first 150 words into a list of 384 numbers. Texts with similar meaning get similar numbers, even when they use different words. 0.45

Both are compared with cosine similarity. The similarity of a visited article $v$ and a candidate article $c$ is their weighted sum:

$$s(v, c) = 0.55\cdot\cos_{\text{text}}(v, c) + 0.45\cdot\cos_{\text{emb}}(v, c)$$

The two measures complement each other: TF-IDF catches exact names and terms, the embedding catches meaning. The weights were chosen by measurement (section 6.2).

Details of the text measure. The word weights come from the whole article, plus the definition counted once more with weight 0.5 (so the words that say what the article is about count more), plus the category words with weight 0.25. Word counts are damped ($1 + \log \text{count}$), and only words that appear in at least two articles are used. Section 6.1 shows that this beats simpler choices.

3.2 From several visited articles to one list¶

People often read about more than one subject. If someone read about Ancient Rome and about geometry, a single average would favour articles halfway between the two (such as History of mathematics) that fit neither subject well. So the tool works in three steps:

  1. Group the visited articles into interests. Visited articles that are similar to each other (mean similarity at least 0.35) form one interest. Ancient Rome and Julius Caesar become one interest, Pythagorean theorem and Euclid another.
  2. Score each candidate by its mean similarity to the articles of an interest, and keep its best interest: $$\text{score}(c) = \max_{\text{interest } I}\ \frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{v \in I} s(v, c)$$
  3. Share the list between interests in proportion to their size, take each interest's best candidates and sort them by score. Articles already visited are never recommended.

If all visited articles are about one subject, they form a single interest, and the score is simply the mean similarity to all of them.

3.3 Explaining a score¶

A score is an average of weighted similarities, so it splits exactly into parts that add up to it:

  • by measure: the text part and the embedding part;
  • by word: the text part is a sum over the words both articles contain, so the words that contribute most can be listed;
  • by visited article: how similar the candidate is to each visited article of its interest.

With $\mathbf{u}$ the mean text vector of the interest and $\mathbf{c}$ the text vector of the candidate:

$$\text{score}(c) = \underbrace{\sum_{\text{words } w} 0.55\, u_w\, c_w}_{\text{text part}} + \underbrace{0.45\cdot\text{mean embedding similarity}}_{\text{embedding part}}$$

Section 4 draws these parts as charts.

4. Example recommendations, with explanations¶

How to read the charts.

  • Score breakdown (two charts side by side): each row is one recommendation and the bar length is its score. On the left the bar is split into the text part (blue) and the embedding part (orange); on the right, into the visited articles it comes from.
  • Single recommendation: on the left, a waterfall of the words that add most to the score, then all other shared words together, then the embedding; the dark bar is the total. On the right, the similarity to each visited article.
  • Heatmap (section 4.2): the similarity of every visited article (rows) to every recommendation (columns).

4.4 Inputs that cannot be used¶

Misspelled titles, disambiguation pages and links outside Wikipedia are skipped with a reason and suggestions. The remaining inputs are still used.

5.1 Article length¶

The horizontal axes are logarithmic: each labelled tick is ten times the previous one.

mean min 10% 50% 90% max
words 5943.0 163.0 1545.0 5196.0 11599.0 22432.0

The median article has about 5,200 words and the longest about 22,400. Preprocessing keeps about half of the words; most of the removed ones are stopwords.

5.2 Most important words¶

The most frequent lemmas (section 2) are general words such as include, century and time. TF-IDF weights say more. The first chart shows the words with the highest average weight over all articles; the second shows, for each topic, the words that stand out most against the rest of the collection.

Each topic is easy to recognise from its words. Two side effects of lemmatization are visible: in People, bear is the lemma of born, and in Geography, mi and sq come from sq mi (square miles).

5.3 Similarity between articles¶

How similar are two random articles? The charts count about 2 million pairs among 2,000 random articles, for each measure and for the combined similarity $s$ (the vertical axis is logarithmic).

  • Text: most pairs share almost no important words, so their similarity is close to 0.
  • Embedding: never close to 0; even unrelated articles have a similarity of about 0.5.
  • Combined: unrelated articles therefore score about 0.2–0.3, and good recommendations about 0.4–0.6. Scores are best read in comparison with each other.

Articles are most similar to others of the same topic (the diagonal). Mathematics is the most self-contained topic. The closest pairs of different topics are Geography and History (countries and empires), and Mathematics and Physical sciences.

6. Evaluation¶

How quality is measured. There are no real users to ask, so a recommended article counts as related if it matches the visited one by information the recommender does not use:

  • same subsection: both are in the same Vital articles subsection;
  • shared category: both have a common Wikipedia category. The categories are split in half; the recommender uses only one half, and this check uses the other.

For each test article we take its 10 most similar articles and compute the share that is related by each rule. The score is the average of the two shares (higher is better). All settings were chosen on one half of the articles, and the results below come from the other half (1,093 articles), so they are not tuned to the test data.

6.1 Which text representation?¶

Each bar is one way of building the TF-IDF word weights:

  • definition only, lead only, full text: which part of the article is used (the lead is the introduction above the first heading);
  • full text + definition: the full text plus the definition counted again (weight 0.5);
  • final (used, in blue): in addition the category words (weight 0.25);
  • ..., stemmed: the same, built from stems instead of lemmas.
  • The whole article works better than its beginning only.
  • Adding the definition and the categories improves on the full text by +0.030.
  • Lemmas beat stems by a small but consistent margin (+0.004 for final, +0.007 for full text), which confirms the choice made in section 2.

6.2 Words, meaning, or both?¶

Each test article is used as a single visited article. text is the TF-IDF measure alone, bge-small the embedding alone, and text + bge-small both together with weights 0.55 and 0.45 (used, in blue).

Using both measures beats text alone by +0.015 and the embedding alone by +0.026. Both differences are statistically significant (their 95 % bootstrap intervals exclude zero).

6.3 Combining several visited articles¶

We simulate 400 users per case, each with a short reading history drawn from the test articles:

  • 1 subject, 3 or 5 articles: all from the same subsection;
  • 2 subjects, 3 + 2 articles: 3 articles on one subject and 2 on an unrelated one. Here the score is averaged with the next panel, so it also rewards serving both subjects;
  • 2 subjects: share of subjects served: how often each of the two subjects gets at least one recommendation (1.0 means always).

Four ways of combining the visited articles are compared:

  • mean (centroid): the average similarity to all visited articles;
  • power mean, p = 4: an average that favours the visited article the candidate is closest to;
  • maximum: only the closest visited article counts;
  • interests, t = 0.35 (used, in blue): the method of section 3.2.
  • One subject: all methods are within 0.03 of each other. Interests and the mean give practically the same result, because a history on one subject usually forms a single interest.
  • Two subjects: grouping into interests is clearly best. It serves both subjects 91 % of the time (mean: 69 %) and raises the score from 0.435 to 0.536.

The threshold t = 0.35 decides when two visited articles belong to the same interest. A lower value merges unrelated articles and behaves like the mean; a higher value splits one subject into pieces. 0.35 worked best on the tuning half.

7. Limitations¶

  • Scores are relative. Unrelated articles still score about 0.2, because embeddings are never far apart. Compare scores with each other; do not read them as probabilities.
  • Only the 2,200 articles can be recommended. An article downloaded on the fly can be used as input, but it is never recommended.
  • Relatedness is approximated. Subsections and categories stand in for what a reader finds related, so surprising but useful recommendations are not rewarded.
  • No diversity control. Within one interest, very similar articles (e.g. Roman Republic and Roman Empire) can both appear.
